sources.title: Reference record · The Large Bathers · Philadelphia version

contentNote: This historical work includes nudity or religious imagery; its context is discussed in the introduction.
story: Bathers occupy a landscape arranged into a large, structured composition. The Philadelphia painting belongs to Cézanne’s sustained investigation of bodies and landscape rather than a record of one observed outing.
how: Arching trees and repeated poses connect the figures to the setting, making the whole composition more important than any single likeness.
details: Trees lean toward one another.
Bodies echo surrounding angles.
Open sky forms a central space.
question: When do bodies begin to function like elements of a landscape?

title: The Boy in the Red Vest
alt: The Boy in the Red Vest by Paul Cézanne. The torso leans toward an arm.

sources.title: Reference record · The Boy in the Red Vest

story: A seated boy in a red vest leans into an absorbed pose. Rather than a polished social performance, the portrait offers an arrangement of color, posture and attention.
how: The strong red garment anchors related planes of color, while the inclined body complicates a simple vertical portrait.
details: The torso leans toward an arm.
The red vest gathers attention.
Cloth and skin are built from patches.
question: How does posture create a mood without a dramatic facial expression?

title: Mont Sainte-Victoire with Large Pine
alt: Mont Sainte-Victoire with Large Pine by Paul Cézanne. A pine frames the nearer view.

sources.title: Reference record · Mont Sainte-Victoire with Large Pine

story: Mont Sainte-Victoire appears within a landscape built from related color patches. This reproduction shows the Courtauld version with a large pine, not every painting in Cézanne’s long mountain series.
how: Near branches and distant mass establish different scales while repeated colors connect the view into a constructed surface.
details: A pine frames the nearer view.
The mountain holds the distance.
Color links separate parts of the landscape.
question: What makes the mountain feel distant without relying on a sharp outline?

credit: Digital reproduction via Wikimedia Commons · Paul Cézanne

title: Still Life with Plaster Cupid
alt: Still Life with Plaster Cupid by Paul Cézanne. The pale sculpture catches light.

sources.title: Reference record · Still Life with Plaster Cupid

story: A plaster Cupid shares a tabletop with fruit and studio objects. A sculpture inside a painting becomes part of a larger question about how surfaces, volumes and viewpoints relate.
how: Tilting planes and strong color relationships make the studio feel assembled through observation rather than fixed by one viewpoint.
details: The pale sculpture catches light.
Fruit echoes rounded bodily forms.
The tabletop seems to change direction.
question: How does a painted sculpture differ from the surrounding painted fruit?

title: The Hanged Man's House
alt: The Hanged Man's House by Paul Cézanne. The road rises between structures.

sources.title: Reference record · The Hanged Man's House

story: A cluster of houses and a steep route form an enclosed landscape. Despite its unsettling traditional title, the painting’s visible subject is a village space organized through material and perspective.
how: Dense paint and angular masses give the buildings weight, while the route provides a narrow movement into the scene.
details: The road rises between structures.
Roofs create related angled planes.
Vegetation and walls have tangible textures.
question: What gives a place a sense of weight?

credit: Digital reproduction via Wikimedia Commons · Mary Cassatt
commonsTitle: File:Mary Cassatt - The Child's Bath - Google Art Project.jpg
title: The Child's Bath
alt: The Child's Bath by Mary Cassatt. The basin forms a clear circle.
story: An adult washes a child in a closely observed domestic act. The high viewpoint and repeated patterns make care visible as both a human relationship and an ambitious composition.
how: Flattened space and patterned surfaces reflect Cassatt’s interest in Japanese prints while remaining a distinct painted scene.
details: The basin forms a clear circle.
Hands connect the figures.
Dress and carpet carry different patterns.
question: How does the elevated viewpoint change your relationship to the act of care?

credit: Digital reproduction via Wikimedia Commons · Mary Cassatt
commonsTitle: File:Cassat - Blue Armchair NGA.jpg
title: Little Girl in a Blue Armchair
alt: Little Girl in a Blue Armchair by Mary Cassatt. Chairs repeat across the room.

sources.title: Reference record · Little Girl in a Blue Armchair

story: A child occupies a large room of blue upholstered chairs. Her relaxed, sprawling pose resists the tidy performance expected of a conventional child portrait.
how: Broad chair shapes and a low, interrupted arrangement give the small figure a setting that feels larger than her immediate attention.
details: Chairs repeat across the room.
The child’s posture is unusually relaxed.
A small dog occupies another seat.
question: Does the room make the child seem free, restless or overwhelmed?

credit: Digital reproduction via Wikimedia Commons · Mary Cassatt
commonsTitle: File:Mary Cassatt - The Boating Party - Google Art Project.jpg
title: The Boating Party
alt: The Boating Party by Mary Cassatt. The boatman faces away.
story: A boatman, a woman and a child occupy a tightly cropped view of a boat. Leisure becomes a structure of large shapes, attention and unequal visual weight.
how: A strong dark figure, bright sail and curving boat edge divide the canvas into bold interlocking areas.
details: The boatman faces away.
The sail is sharply cropped.
A curved rim gathers the passengers.
question: How does the figure with his back to us shape our access to the others?

credit: Digital reproduction via Wikimedia Commons · Mary Cassatt
commonsTitle: File:Mary Stevenson Cassatt - In the Loge - Google Art Project.jpg
title: In the Loge
alt: In the Loge by Mary Cassatt. Opera glasses extend the woman’s gaze.
story: A woman looks through opera glasses in a theater while another spectator looks toward her. The image turns spectatorship itself into a social subject.
how: The woman’s dark clothing and the balcony’s curve establish a strong near plane against the layered audience beyond.
details: Opera glasses extend the woman’s gaze.
Another viewer directs attention toward her.
The balcony separates public and private-looking space.
question: Who is looking, and who is being looked at?

credit: Digital reproduction via Wikimedia Commons · Mary Cassatt
commonsTitle: File:Young Mother Sewing MET DP139632.jpg
title: Young Mother Sewing
alt: Young Mother Sewing by Mary Cassatt. The adult’s hands remain occupied.
story: A woman sews while a child leans against her. The Met records that two unrelated models posed for the painting, a useful reminder that a convincing domestic scene can be constructed.
how: Different directions of attention connect care, work and independent childhood interest without making every gaze agree.
details: The adult’s hands remain occupied.
The child looks outward.
The fabric connects the figures physically.
question: Does knowing the scene was posed change its emotional effect?

credit: Digital reproduction via Wikimedia Commons · Mary Cassatt
commonsTitle: File:Breakfast in Bed (1897) by Mary Cassatt, Huntington Library.jpg
title: Breakfast in Bed
alt: Breakfast in Bed by Mary Cassatt. The mother looks toward the child.
story: A mother holds a child in bed, but their gazes lead in different directions. The scene combines closeness with the child’s interest in a world beyond the embrace.
how: Large pale bedding and tightly cropped figures make a familiar morning subject into a carefully arranged field of shapes.
details: The mother looks toward the child.
The child looks beyond her.
Bedding expands around the figures.
question: Can an embrace contain two different centers of attention?

credit: Digital reproduction via Wikimedia Commons · Mary Cassatt
commonsTitle: File:Mary Cassatt - Summertime - TFAA 1988.25.jpg
title: Summertime
alt: Summertime by Mary Cassatt. The boat’s rim cuts a strong curve.
story: Two women share a small boat on summer water. The quiet subject gives Cassatt room to explore cropping, reflected light and the social space between companions.
how: A high viewpoint and flat areas of color organize figures and boat into an unusually immediate composition.
details: The boat’s rim cuts a strong curve.
Water fills much of the setting.
The figures remain close but distinct.
question: What makes the air or water feel like summer?

credit: Digital reproduction via Wikimedia Commons · Wassily Kandinsky
commonsTitle: File:Composition VII - Wassily Kandinsky, GAC.jpg
title: Composition VII
alt: Composition VII by Wassily Kandinsky. Curves and diagonals collide.
story: Dense color and interwoven forms resist a single recognizable scene. The painting belongs to Kandinsky’s early abstract period, when composition could suggest a powerful event without illustrating a conventional story.
how: Overlapping directional marks and contrasting colors make the surface feel active across many points rather than organized around one object.
details: Curves and diagonals collide.
Warm and cool colors alternate.
Some boundaries dissolve into neighboring forms.
question: Can you follow a route through the painting without naming what you see?

credit: Digital reproduction via Wikimedia Commons · Wassily Kandinsky
commonsTitle: File:Kandinsky - Composition 8, July 1923.jpg
title: Composition VIII
location: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York
alt: Composition VIII by Wassily Kandinsky. Large and small circles create different weights.
story: Circles, lines and angular forms interact on a pale ground. Painted during Kandinsky’s Bauhaus years, this composition presents a more geometric language than the turbulent Composition VII.
how: Differences in size, spacing and direction create relationships that can feel dynamic even without a depicted event.
details: Large and small circles create different weights.
Diagonals cross calmer forms.
Open space separates competing groups.
question: Which shape feels heaviest, and what gives it that weight?

credit: Digital reproduction via Wikimedia Commons · Wassily Kandinsky
commonsTitle: File:Kandinsky - Jaune Rouge Bleu.jpg
title: Yellow–Red–Blue
alt: Yellow–Red–Blue by Wassily Kandinsky. Yellow dominates a more angular area.
story: A yellow angular zone and a large blue circular form occupy contrasting areas, with red and many smaller elements connecting them. The title directs attention to color without supplying a literal scene.
how: Color, geometry and freely curving lines work together rather than behaving as one rigid system.
details: Yellow dominates a more angular area.
Blue gathers into a large circle.
Small curves complicate the geometry.
question: Do colors seem to advance or recede as you look between them?

credit: Digital reproduction via Wikimedia Commons · Wassily Kandinsky
commonsTitle: File:Vassily Kandinsky, 1926 - Several Circles, Gugg 0910 25.jpg
title: Several Circles
location: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York
alt: Several Circles by Wassily Kandinsky. Some circles overlap transparently.
story: Colored circles overlap against a dark field. The limited vocabulary of shapes produces surprisingly varied relationships among transparency, scale and visual weight.
how: Differences in diameter, color and overlap make circles appear to gather, hover and interrupt one another.
details: Some circles overlap transparently.
A large circle organizes the field.
Small colored forms suggest different distances.
question: Does the dark field feel flat, deep or something in between?

credit: Digital reproduction via Wikimedia Commons · Wassily Kandinsky
commonsTitle: File:Wassily Kandinsky, 1903, The Blue Rider (Der Blaue Reiter), oil on canvas, 52.1 x 54.6 cm, Stiftung Sammlung E.G. Bührle, Zurich.jpg
title: The Blue Rider
alt: The Blue Rider by Wassily Kandinsky. The rider forms a compact accent.
story: A rider crosses a landscape in a small painting from before Kandinsky’s mature abstraction. The recognizable subject makes it useful for noticing continuity as well as change in his career.
how: Broken color and a simplified rider connect an observed landscape with an increasingly expressive handling of the surface.
details: The rider forms a compact accent.
The slope gives movement a direction.
Light and shadow break into patches.
question: What remains recognizable, and what is already becoming a pattern?

credit: Digital reproduction via Wikimedia Commons · Wassily Kandinsky
commonsTitle: File:Vassily Kandinsky, 1923 - On White II.jpg
title: On White II
alt: On White II by Wassily Kandinsky. Dark diagonals establish opposing directions.
story: Angular dark forms and colored elements cross a pale field. The painting belongs to Kandinsky’s geometric experiments rather than a depiction of an ordinary room or landscape.
how: Crossing diagonals create tension, while smaller colored shapes and surrounding white keep the structure from becoming uniformly heavy.
details: Dark diagonals establish opposing directions.
Small colors interrupt the pale field.
White remains an active interval.
question: How can empty-looking space take part in a composition?
